articles.title: 🪪 Identity-Verification Company Loses 150 Million Driver's Licenses From Its Cloud; The One Firm Whose Entire Job Was Proving Who You Are Has Misplaced Everyone
articles.dateline: THE BREACH — reported from a very sheepish press conference
paras: A company whose sole purpose is verifying that people are who they claim to be confirmed that more than 150 million driver's licenses were stolen from its cloud storage — an incident with the perfect, terrible symmetry of a locksmith leaving every key in the city on a park bench.

"We take this breach extremely seriously," the company said, of a business model that now consists of apologizing to the entire population whose identities it was paid to guard. Experts note the special irony of 2026: we built an industry to prove you are you, entrusted it with the one document that says so, and it promptly handed the lot to the exact people you were trying to keep it from. Somewhere, a scan of your face is having a wonderful, unauthorized day.

articles.title: ⚡ A.I. Data Centers Are Now Measured In Gigawatts; We Have Started Sizing Our Computers The Way We Size Power Plants, Because They Basically Are
articles.dateline: THE OUTBACK — reported beside two gigawatts of humming metal
paras: A chip giant announced plans for enormous new "A.I. factories" abroad, describing them not in terms of processors or square footage but in gigawatts — the same unit used for nuclear plants — quietly confirming that the modern computer has grown so hungry it is now measured by how much of the national grid it eats.

"It's the infrastructure of intelligence," the company said, of facilities rated like power stations because, functionally, they compete with them. Analysts note the quiet threshold we've crossed: a data center used to be a room you kept cool, and is now a load-bearing part of a country's electricity supply, which is either the dawn of a new industrial age or simply the largest space heater ever constructed.

articles.title: 📋 State Launches An Official Registry Of A.I. Auditors; The Hottest New Career Is Professionally Checking The Robots' Homework
articles.dateline: THE STATE CAPITOL — reported from a freshly printed clipboard
paras: A large state unveiled a plan to create an official registry of certified A.I. auditors — accredited professionals whose job is to inspect A.I. systems and confirm they are behaving — thereby inventing an entire respectable career out of double-checking the machines we built specifically so we wouldn't have to check things.

"Accountability requires oversight," officials said, of a role that amounts to a hall monitor for algorithms. Experts note the reassuring, slightly absurd shape of progress: we automated the work to save human effort, discovered the automation needed watching, and so hired a fresh batch of humans to watch it — a solution that is either wise governance or the world's most sophisticated way of giving people their jobs back.

articles.title: 🛒 Big Tech Firm Buys Yet Another A.I. Startup; The Acquisition Is The Product, And The Product Is Quietly Switched Off
articles.dateline: THE CAP TABLE — reported from an empty office with great furniture
paras: A tech giant announced it had acquired another promising A.I. startup, continuing a year-long shopping spree in which the industry's biggest players scoop up small teams — a modern ritual where the thing being purchased is the talent, and the beloved little product they built is gently escorted to the exit.

"We're excited to welcome the team," the buyer said, of a deal that will end with the startup's app displaying a fond farewell message within the year. Analysts note the emerging life cycle of the A.I. startup: raise money, build something people love, get bought for the brains behind it, and watch your creation become a heartfelt blog post titled "An Update On Our Journey." It is the circle of life, if the lion also owned the savanna.

articles.title: 🔍 Government Opens A File On The Dominant Chipmaker; Regulators Have Finally Noticed That One Company Quietly Owns The Whole Picture
articles.dateline: WASHINGTON — reported from a very large manila folder
paras: Regulators confirmed they have opened an inquiry into the world's most dominant chipmaker, a company so central to the A.I. boom that nearly every advance of the past few years has, in some form, passed through its silicon — a level of control that has finally attracted the kind of official attention that arrives with subpoenas.

"We're reviewing the competitive landscape," officials said, of a landscape in which the competition largely rents its ground from a single landlord. Analysts note the government's timing has a familiar flavor: the concern arrives only once a company has grown so essential that acting against it might break the very thing everyone depends on — the regulatory equivalent of noticing the horse has bolted, and thoughtfully forming a committee about the barn.

horoscopes.text: The company that keeps your ID safe will lose it today. There is nothing you can do. Change nothing; you own nothing anyway. Carry on.
A new job will be invented near you to watch a machine that replaced an old job. Apply. The circle continues, and the pay is good.
A data center near a distant country will draw two gigawatts today. Your phone still dies at 4pm. The universe is not fair. Charge it.

tech_tip: Before you trust a company to guard your ID, ask where it stores 150 million of them. Before you fear the robots, remember someone now audits them for a living. 2026 breaks things, then invents a job to inspect the breakage.
gadget_watch: No new gadget this week — just a data center the size of a power plant, an app about to be quietly switched off after its makers got bought, and a leaked copy of your driver's license enjoying a life of its own somewhere online. Your gadgets are fine. Your data, less so.

classifieds.text: You: my digital identity, now owned by strangers. Me: the actual me, still here, unable to prove it. If you see us both, only one is real. It's me.
